title: Insects
intro: Hi! I'm Angélica, the forest ranger. Today we start getting to know insects: what they are, what their bodies are like and how they eat. No need to be scared, just curious!

lessons.title: What is an insect?
lessons.intro: Today we find out what makes a bug an insect. Count legs with me!
lessons.closing: Insects have six legs, three body parts and a hard skeleton on the outside. With that you can already tell them apart from other bugs, like spiders, which also catch flies and mosquitoes.

exercises.prompt: Which ones are insects? Tap all the ones with six legs.
exercises.explanation: The spider has eight legs, so it is not an insect. Insects have six.

exercises.prompt: How many legs does an insect have?
exercises.explanation: Six legs: three pairs, and all of them come out of the thorax.

exercises.prompt: What makes an insect's body hard on the outside?
exercises.explanation: Chitin forms its exoskeleton: a hard skeleton on the outside, like armor.

exercises.prompt: Tap all the insects.
exercises.explanation: The centipede has lots and lots of legs and the spider has eight. Insects always have six.

exercises.prompt: True or false? All insects have wings.
exercises.explanation: Almost all have one or two pairs of wings, but some have none.

lessons.title: Head, thorax and abdomen
lessons.intro: An insect's body is divided into three parts. Let's find them on an ant.
lessons.closing: Head, thorax and abdomen: three parts that are easy to remember. When you see a bug with a body in three parts, you know it's probably an insect.

exercises.prompt: Put each name in its place.
exercises.explanation: From top to bottom: head, thorax and abdomen.

exercises.prompt: Which part holds the legs and the wings?
exercises.explanation: The wings come out of the top of the thorax and the legs out of the bottom.

exercises.prompt: Where are the antennae and the eyes?
exercises.explanation: The head has a pair of antennae, the eyes and the mouth.

exercises.prompt: Match each part with what it has.
exercises.explanation: The head senses and eats, the thorax moves the body and the abdomen holds the heart and digestion.

exercises.prompt: Into how many parts is an insect's body divided?
exercises.explanation: Three: head, thorax and abdomen.

lessons.title: Legs and wings
lessons.intro: Six legs and, almost always, wings. Let's see how many!
lessons.closing: Insect legs can be for running, jumping, swimming or holding on. And wings let them live almost anywhere on the planet.

exercises.prompt: How many pairs of legs does an insect have?
exercises.explanation: Three pairs: six legs in total.

exercises.prompt: Which part of the body do the wings come out of?
exercises.explanation: The wings are attached to the top of the thorax.

exercises.prompt: How many pairs of wings do insects usually have?
exercises.explanation: Usually two pairs. Some have only one and others have none.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Insects have ___ legs and usually ___ pairs of wings.
exercises.explanation: Six legs and, usually, two pairs of wings.

exercises.prompt: True or false? All insects have two pairs of wings.
exercises.explanation: Some have only one pair and others have no wings.

lessons.title: Antennae and senses
lessons.intro: Insects sense the world in a very different way from us. Let's find out how!
lessons.closing: Insects smell with their antennae and feel with their whole body. So a moving antenna is not a threat: it's a bug exploring what's around it.

exercises.prompt: Match each sense with what it does.

pairs.right: Detect faint smells in the air
Hear and feel with the whole body

exercises.explanation: Antennae to smell, hairs to hear and feel, and eyes with many lenses.

exercises.prompt: For insects, what matters more?
exercises.explanation: Smells and tastes tell them where food is and who another insect is.

exercises.prompt: Which part of the body do they use to detect smells in the air?
exercises.explanation: Antennae move around and pick up very faint smells.

exercises.prompt: Insects see less than we do, but they are better at noticing...
exercises.explanation: They detect movement very well, that's why they react so fast.

exercises.prompt: Crickets hear with tiny ears. Where are they?
exercises.explanation: Crickets have ears on their front legs. Other insects have them on the abdomen or wings, and many have no ears at all: they feel sound with tiny hairs.

lessons.title: How do they eat?
lessons.intro: Each insect eats in its own way. Today we find out why some sting or bite and others chew.
lessons.closing: An insect that bites does it to feed or to defend itself, not because it's bad. If you understand how it eats, you understand why it does what it does.

exercises.prompt: Match each mouthpart with how it works.

pairs.right: A needle to pierce and suck

exercises.explanation: Chewing to cut, sucking to drink and piercing-sucking to pierce and suck.

exercises.prompt: A butterfly drinks flower nectar through a tube. What mouthparts does it have?
exercises.explanation: Sucking: it drinks liquids like nectar.

exercises.prompt: A grasshopper cuts leaves with its jaws. What mouthparts does it have?
exercises.explanation: Chewing: it uses jaws with sharp edges, like plant eaters do.

exercises.prompt: A mosquito bites with a kind of needle to suck blood. What mouthparts does it have?
exercises.explanation: Piercing-sucking: it pierces and sucks. It bites to eat, not to attack you.

exercises.prompt: Look at each insect's mouth and put it in its box.
exercises.explanation: Jaws to bite, a coiled tube to drink and a needle to pierce.

exam.title: Unit challenge
exam.intro: Challenge time! Ten mixed questions. If you pass, you open the next unit.
exam.closing: Now you know what an insect is, what its body is like and how it eats! A forest ranger observes, isn't afraid and respects every animal.

exercises.prompt: Tap all the insects.
exercises.explanation: The spider has eight legs. Insects have six.

exercises.prompt: How many legs does an insect have?
exercises.explanation: Six legs, three pairs.

exercises.prompt: Put each name in its place.
exercises.explanation: From top to bottom: head, thorax and abdomen.

exercises.prompt: Which part of the body holds the legs and the wings?
exercises.explanation: The thorax is the middle part: the six legs and the wings come out of it, like branches from a trunk.

exercises.prompt: What is the hard skeleton that covers an insect's body made of?
exercises.explanation: Chitin forms its exoskeleton.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: The ___ detect smells in the air.
exercises.explanation: Antennae move around and pick up faint smells.

exercises.prompt: True or false? All insects have wings.
exercises.explanation: False: almost all have wings, but some have none, like worker ants or fleas.

exercises.prompt: Match each mouthpart with how it works.

pairs.right: A needle to pierce and suck

exercises.explanation: Cut, drink or pierce: each insect has the mouthparts it needs.

exercises.prompt: A butterfly drinks nectar through a tube. What mouthparts does it have?
exercises.explanation: Sucking: a butterfly's tongue is a long tube, like a straw, that curls up when it isn't drinking.

exercises.prompt: An insect's compound eye has many...
exercises.explanation: Many lenses that work like mini-eyes.
